target_recommendation.pool_cutoff_note: UNCHANGED 2026-08-30 (session 7) - deliberately kept distinct from snapshot above (T4, not T3). Matches card_pool.cutoff exactly (already an independent top-level field, untouched by this correction). CORRECTED 2026-08-30 (session 8): the recommended legality_basis for a future canonical pool is 'community-retrospective', not 'historical-policy' - see pool_legality_basis_recommendation and historical_event_pool_legality_status below for the full derivation and the reasoning this replaces. In short: schemas/pool.schema.json's historical-policy value 'requires period policy evidence for its exceptions'; this research chain has none - only an absence-of-evidence finding ('no source establishes Aug-26-distributed cards were tournament-legal that same day') plus one card's (Gate Guardian's) incidental technical unusability (its Fusion Materials did not exist yet) - neither of which is evidence that period POLICY excluded Aug-26 products; 'no evidence X was legal' is not 'evidence policy prohibited X'. community-retrospective fits what actually exists: a modern community convention ('day before the event', matching the community's own established snapshot and the ygoprodeck-tokyo-dome-cube cross-check already in card_pool.community_cross_check), which the schema explicitly permits to 'deliberately differ from what was registerable at the historical event' without requiring period-policy proof - exactly this repository's own GOAT and Edison pool precedent (both data/pools/*.json files are tagged legality_basis: 'community-retrospective', confirmed by direct read).

historical_event_pool_legality_status.proposition: Distinct from pool_legality_basis_recommendation above: NOT 'what legality_basis label should a future canonical pool carry' (that is resolved - community-retrospective, per schema/precedent, regardless of this question's answer), but 'did actual 1999-08-26 Tokyo Dome tournament deck-registration policy permit or exclude cards first distributed that same day' - a genuine historical-policy question in its own right, independent of and NOT gating the pool recommendation, which is deliberately community-retrospective precisely BECAUSE this question is unresolved.
historical_event_pool_legality_status.what_is_known: No source located by this research chain establishes that any Aug-26-distributed card WAS legal for use in tournament decks played that same day (P1: absence of evidence of legality). Separately, the Gate Guardian attendance/participation promo specifically is affirmatively evidenced to have been UNUSABLE in any coherent deck at the event, because its Fusion Material monsters were not released until 1999-09-23 (V Jump Vol.5) - a full month later. This is real, but narrow: it demonstrates ONE card was practically unplayable for a combo-piece-availability reason specific to that card, not that tournament POLICY excluded Aug-26 products as a category (P2). No source establishes P2 either way.
historical_event_pool_legality_status.what_is_unknown: Whether 1999-08-26 tournament deck-registration policy (a) permitted any card physically available that day regardless of distribution channel, (b) excluded same-day-distributed cards as a category, or (c) excluded them only incidentally case-by-case (as Gate Guardian's own missing-combo-pieces problem illustrates, without that being a POLICY reason). None of the three is proven. Consequently, whether the exact 370-card candidate pool (built on the community-retrospective 1999-08-25 convention) matches what was ACTUALLY registerable at the real event is not yet proven either way - the pool could be exactly right, could be missing legally-registerable Aug-26 cards, or (per Gate Guardian) could in principle already correctly exclude at least one card for the right underlying reason (practical unusability) even though the STATED reason (a blanket same-day exclusion) is not itself proven as policy.
historical_event_pool_legality_status.provenance_of_the_only_located_evidence: The Gate Guardian finding lives at superseded_findings.rejected_2026_08_rules_and_restriction_research.event_day_pool_interaction - ARCHIVED, not live/current authoritative data (confirmed by direct JSON-path walk: nested under a key literally named superseded_findings). Its own conclusion is explicitly a precautionary default under uncertainty ('per the task's explicit instruction not to infer "released at the event" = "legal in the event" absent proof'), not a discovered historical-policy fact - citing it as if it independently established a period-policy rule (as an earlier version of this packet's prose did) overclaimed what even the archived source itself claims.
historical_event_pool_legality_status.what_would_resolve_this: A contemporaneous 1999 Konami/tournament-organizer deck-registration rule, entry regulation, or equivalent period document that explicitly states whether cards distributed at the event were immediately tournament-legal. Absent that, this remains UNRESOLVED - and, per this pass's central principle, must not be silently promoted to a policy claim on the strength of an evidentiary gap alone.
historical_event_pool_legality_status.does_not_block: This status does NOT gate target_recommendation.pool_legality_basis_recommendation (community-retrospective is independently correct regardless of this question's answer - it is precisely the legality_basis value the schema provides for exactly this situation), does NOT change the certified 370-card pool membership or its digest, and is not one of restriction_list_current's canonicalization axes (it concerns the card_pool/target_recommendation object, a different research question from the restriction list's own content/scope/effective-date facts).

format_identity.snapshot_rationale: The task's instruction was to reassess the pre-event snapshot only if evidence proves the historically meaningful playable snapshot should instead be event-day and include same-day cards. This swarm found no such evidence; if anything it found evidence CUTTING AGAINST event-day cleanliness: (1) Agent B/E independently found multiple convergent-but-hedge-heavy retrospective sources (5+ independent Japanese blogs beyond what Agent B alone found) describing the event as disrupted by overcrowding severe enough to require riot police, with a live claim that the finals tournament itself may not have concluded at the venue that day and were possibly re-held regionally later - zero primary/contemporaneous (period newspaper, Konami statement) confirmation was found either way, by either agent, despite deliberate searching. (2) Directly verified against live repo state this session (not merely asserted): Gate Guardian, the events own headline attendance promo card, is ABSENT from the certified 370-card pre-event pool - and so are all three of its Fusion Material monsters (Suijin, Kazejin, Sanga of the Thunder), confirmed by recomputing retroformats.releases.evaluate_cutoff against the certified 1999-08-25 cutoff and checking all four names directly (none present in the 370). This means Gate Guardian could not have been Fusion Summoned by anyone restricted to the certified pre-event pool, regardless of exactly when its materials were later released. Cross-referenced (medium confidence, multi-source WebSearch corroboration since a direct Konami-database fetch could not complete in this sandbox - see source_bibliography) against community card-list aggregators converging on Vol.5, 1999-09-23 as the materials actual first OCG-JP release, a full month after Tokyo Dome - consistent with, though not required to support, the repo-verified absence finding. Both findings make 'the format played that day' a more fragile historical anchor than the pre-event certified-release-ledger snapshot, which rests on the repo's own independently re-verified, twice-audited (recertified commit 334f5865) product chronology. The pre-event 1999-08-25, 370-card snapshot remains the recommended and safer choice.
event_completion_caveat: NEW, significant finding not present in the prior gate: whether the Tokyo Dome tournament final actually concluded at the venue on August 26, 1999 as commonly assumed is itself in genuine doubt per multiple independent (but all retrospective, hedge-heavy, oral-history-based) Japanese community sources describing a crowd-control failure, riot police, cancelled Premium Pack sales, and a claim the finals never took place / were re-held regionally. No period (1999) documentary source was located by either Agent B or Agent E despite dedicated searching in both English and Japanese. This does not change the certified pre-event 370-card pool (which does not depend on the event concluding) but is material to any future claim that 'the Tokyo Dome format' represents a coherent, completed, single-day competitive event - it may represent a competitive structure that was announced and partially run, not one that cleanly concluded. Reported as an open historical question, not resolved either way.

scope_dispute.finding: NEW in this pass (found by Agent E, not surfaced by A/B/C): the two sources this packet already cites for the 3-card restriction list - Yugipedia and ocg-card.com - describe DIFFERENT OBJECTS when read closely. Yugipedia's page frames the 3-card list as Konami's first OFFICIAL nationwide restriction list, implicitly applicable to all sanctioned OCG play. ocg-card.com's page (an independent Japanese cataloguing site, not Konami) frames what looks like the same 3 cards as a TOURNAMENT-SPECIFIC rule sheet tied to a named 1999 regional/qualifying event, not a blanket nationwide restriction. Neither page cites a Konami-original document; both are downstream retrospectives. This produces a genuine three-way ambiguity: (a) nationwide official restriction list in force for ALL Japanese OCG play by Aug 1999, (b) a tournament-specific ruleset for one or more qualifying events that may or may not have applied at Tokyo Dome itself, (c) a modern community retro-format convention retrofitted onto 1999 with no 1999-dated basis at all. The swarm could not adjudicate between these three readings - no source examined states which one is correct, and no contemporaneous (1999) Konami document was located by any agent.
scope_dispute.adjudication: Applying the evidence hierarchy: both cited sources sit at tier 5-6 (specialist community research / semi-generic wiki), well below the tier-1/2 contemporaneous-official material the hierarchy prioritizes. Since the two available tier-5/6 sources actively disagree on SCOPE (not just on details within a shared scope), the hierarchy gives no basis to prefer one over the other - this is a genuine evidentiary tie at the lowest tiers, not a case where a higher-tier source resolves a lower-tier disagreement. Per the task's explicit instruction ('if evidence can't support an exact complete list, do NOT invent one - mark canonicalization BLOCKED' and 'model ordinary-OCG-restrictions vs Tokyo-Dome-tournament-restrictions vs later-retro-format-community-convention SEPARATELY if they differ'), this is exactly that condition: the three readings differ in ways that matter (nationwide legal restriction vs one-event tournament rule vs modern retrofit) and cannot be collapsed into one list without guessing which the sources meant.

restriction_list_research.verdict_detail: Restriction-list CONTENT (Raigeki/Dark Hole/Trap Hole, Limited-to-1, single-tier) is well-corroborated across independent sources and is NOT in dispute. Restriction-list SCOPE (nationwide-OCG vs Tokyo-Dome-tournament-only vs modern-retrofit) IS in dispute between the two best available sources and cannot be resolved with currently available evidence. Canonicalization of a restriction list for this format is therefore BLOCKED per the task's explicit instruction, pending discovery of a contemporaneous (tier 1-3) source that states which of the three scopes is correct.

classified_rules.rationale: DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 is the only related flag. It removes the Main Phase 2 window entirely, which happens to match '1999 had no Main Phase 2' at a surface level, but the already-run test_tokyo_dome_rules.py experiment found DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 also removes a distinct post-battle legal action window the actual 1999 single-Main-Phase model never had to begin with (period rules allowed certain post-battle actions inside the single Main Phase's continuation, not a discrete second phase) - so the flag changes MORE than the history requires in one direction while getting the headline behavior right in another. Classified as approximated, not exact, and this gap was already flagged in this packet's existing architecture.gaps before this pass; this pass CONFIRMS rather than newly discovers it.

DUEL_ATTACK_FIRST_TURN's companion no-draw-on-first-turn behavior is a direct flag-level match already exercised in tests/engine/test_historical_behaviour.py per the harness constants read this session.

DUEL_ATTACK_FIRST_TURN exists and can toggle this at the engine level, so the ENGINE side is exactly representable either way - but rule_chronology above found the historical fact itself (was first-turn attack legal at the Aug 25/26 1999 boundary) is unresolved between agents. Classification therefore tracks the historical unknown, not an engine limitation.

superseded_content._purpose: Phase A of the 2026-08-30 (session 5) re-derivation pass: before doing more source research, this repository's own banlist schema, validator, and existing GOAT/Edison/Tengu examples were read to determine EXACTLY what a canonical banlist date represents and what propositions an August-26-Tokyo-Dome event-specific snapshot artifact would actually require - rather than assuming the prior session's three-axis (content/scope/effective-date) threshold was the correct one. Every claim below cites the exact schema field, code line, or doc passage it is derived from - per this pass's explicit instruction, nothing here is inferred without a citation.

A1_what_effective_date_means.schema_text: schemas/banlist.schema.json: banlist title/description is "One historical Forbidden/Limited list as it took effect on a given date." effective_date is an isoDate; superseded_by_date is nullable, "Date the next list took effect, if known. null when unknown or still current."
A1_what_effective_date_means.doc_text: docs/format-schema.md, Banlist section: "`effective_date` and `superseded_by_date` let the validator prove the list was actually in force on a format's snapshot date." (verbatim)
A1_what_effective_date_means.mechanical_check: retroformats/validate.py, _validate_format (~line 1715-1728): `eff = self._date(banlist.effective_date)`; `if eff and snapshot and not (eff <= snapshot): error("format.banlist-not-in-force", ...)` - i.e. the format's OWN period.snapshot date must be ON OR AFTER the banlist's effective_date, or validation fails. Symmetrically, `superseded = self._date(banlist.raw.get("superseded_by_date"))`; `if superseded and snapshot and snapshot >= superseded: error("format.banlist-superseded", ...)` - the snapshot must be BEFORE the list was superseded.
A1_what_effective_date_means.mechanical_use_in_build: retroformats/lflist.py build_lflist()/_build_whitelist(): reads banlist.entries (the card/status list) and fmt's own errata selection - banlist.effective_date is NEVER read by the build path at all. It exists purely for the validator's format<->banlist consistency check described above, not to drive any generated byte in dist/.
A1_what_effective_date_means.conclusion: effective_date means: the date THIS SPECIFIC BANLIST SNAPSHOT (this exact combination of forbidden/limited/semilimited entries) took effect, used ONLY to prove that a format referencing it has its own representative snapshot date falling inside [effective_date, superseded_by_date). It does NOT mean "the first historical date this restriction concept ever began" (a banlist revision date is definitionally the date THIS list, possibly a later revision of an earlier policy, took effect) - and for a format whose snapshot IS the effective_date itself (the common case; see period.snapshot precedent below), the two can legitimately be the same value without requiring any deeper chronological research.
A1_what_effective_date_means.existing_precedent: formats/2005-04-goat/format.json: period.start = period.snapshot = "2005-04-01" = data/banlists/tcg/2005-04.json's own effective_date. The format's own notes field says plainly: "period.start is that list's effective date... snapshot=start is a modeling choice." The GOAT banlist's OWN notes field additionally says "the effective/superseded dates are the community-documented April 1 / October 1 2005 TCG list boundaries and ALSO NEED A PRIMARY CITATION" (emphasis added) - i.e. this repository has ALREADY canonicalized and shipped a banlist (GOAT) whose own effective_date rests on community-documented sourcing, not a personally-authenticated primary 2005 document. This is direct precedent, not merely a hypothetical, for the evidentiary bar this project actually applies to effective_date in practice.

A2_minimum_propositions_for_an_august_26.content_membership: LOAD-BEARING / REQUIRED. Feeds banlist.entries directly (schema: entries[].card + entries[].status) - this is the actual byte-level content of the artifact. Positive claim: each of the 3 named cards IS restricted to the stated status.
A2_minimum_propositions_for_an_august_26.content_completeness: LOAD-BEARING / REQUIRED, and NOT automatically satisfied by content_membership. Schema: "Cards not listed are unlimited (3 copies)" - i.e. an incomplete banlist.entries doesn't fail to build, it SILENTLY misrepresents a 4th restricted card as unlimited. Positive membership of 3 known cards is a different proposition from "these 3 are the ONLY restricted cards" - see Phase G.
A2_minimum_propositions_for_an_august_26.target_event_applicability: LOAD-BEARING / REQUIRED. This is what justifies setting effective_date <= the format's own period.snapshot (the event date, 1999-08-26) in the first place, per the A1 mechanical check above. Evidence must show these specific restrictions were in force AT the August 26 Tokyo Dome target, not merely that a restriction existed somewhere/sometime in 1999.
A2_minimum_propositions_for_an_august_26.effective_date_value: A REQUIRED SCHEMA FIELD (isoDate, required by banlist.schema.json), but the VALUE it needs is NOT "the first-ever historical date this restriction began." Per A1's mechanical check, any date d with d <= 1999-08-26 that is defensibly this list's effective date passes validation - including the event date itself, 1999-08-26, if target_event_applicability is the only proposition proven. Choosing an earlier date (e.g. if V Jump's ~1999-07-21 publication date were authenticated) would be a legitimate STRENGTHENING, not a requirement.
A2_minimum_propositions_for_an_august_26.outer_scope_h2_vs_h3: NOT LOAD-BEARING for an August-26-snapshot artifact. See the critical_logical_test below for the demonstration. Retained as historical research metadata, explicitly marked non-blocking.
A2_minimum_propositions_for_an_august_26.first_effective_date_true_origin: NOT LOAD-BEARING beyond what effective_date_value already requires (a defensible date <= snapshot). Resolving exactly when the restriction FIRST began (mid-July? early August? at qualifiers?) would only matter if we wanted to claim an EARLIER effective_date than the conservative default of the event date itself - it is a strengthening opportunity, not a blocker, for THIS artifact.
A2_minimum_propositions_for_an_august_26.source_authentication: LOAD-BEARING at this project's own evidentiary bar for the propositions that ARE load-bearing above (content_membership, content_completeness, target_event_applicability). Per schemas/common.schema.json implementationStatus enum: "verified: complete AND the load-bearing historical claims are corroborated by strong primary/period evidence (archived official pages, period policy documents, period coverage) - not merely by modern community consensus." This is the cross-cutting question of whether ANY source in the current evidence base actually meets that bar, independent of which specific proposition it is being cited for.

critical_logical_test.question: Would choosing H2 (August 26 Tokyo Dome finals only) versus H3 (the whole national tournament run, including qualifying rounds before the finals) change one byte of a proposed period.snapshot="1999-08-26" banlist artifact?
critical_logical_test.answer: NO, demonstrated as follows. (1) banlist.entries would be identical under H2 or H3 - the same 3 cards, same statuses, are in force AT the August 26 finals either way; H3 only adds that the SAME restriction ALSO applied earlier/elsewhere, which adds no new entries and changes no existing entry's status. (2) effective_date would not need to differ either: per A1, effective_date only needs to satisfy effective_date <= snapshot (1999-08-26). Under H2, the restriction is proven in force starting no later than 1999-08-26 itself - effective_date = "1999-08-26" is fully defensible and schema-valid. Under H3, the restriction was ALSO in force earlier (e.g. during qualifiers), which would let effective_date legitimately move EARLIER if we chose to claim it - but choosing not to claim an earlier date and instead using the same conservative "1999-08-26" value remains equally valid under H3. H2-vs-H3 therefore changes AT MOST the earliest defensible value of effective_date, never a required one, and never any entries. (3) No other field in banlist.schema.json or format.schema.json reads H2-vs-H3 at all. CONCLUSION: H2-vs-H3 is real, valuable, currently-unresolved historical research (see outer_scope_status) but is NOT a canonicalization blocker for this specific artifact - retaining it as a blocker was conflating a historically-interesting open question with an artifact requirement, exactly the failure mode this pass was asked to check for.

corrected_claims.correction: WRONG. The original Starter Box rulebook does not use an immediate deck-out loss. It states explicitly: when a player's Deck is emptied and they cannot draw, the Duel is instead decided by comparing remaining Life Points, with the higher-LP player winning. Modern ocgcore's hardcoded default (drawing from an empty Deck is an immediate loss) does NOT match this and cannot be reconfigured to produce an LP-comparison outcome via any documented DUEL_* flag or OCG_Player field. Corrected classification: NOT_REPRESENTABLE. This restores and confirms the earlier (pre-2026-08) hardening gate's own conclusion that deck-out is a serious, genuine engine gap - the 2026-08 rules-research pass had incorrectly overwritten that with 'exactly representable', which this corrective pass reverses.

corrected_claims.correction: WRONG. The original Starter Box rulebook states explicitly: 'Each Duel starts with each player having 8000 points.' This is PROVEN for the Starter Box tier, personally re-verified by the adjudicator. 2000 LP does not appear anywhere in the 1999 OCG rulebook - it is a figure associated with an unrelated manga/anime 'Basic Rules' depiction, not the real tabletop OCG rule, and must not be used as a stand-in for it. corrected_claims.prior_claim: engine_representability entries[Single Main Phase (no Main Phase 2)] said DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 is 'APPROXIMATED' because it 'removes a post-battle action window the actual 1999 single-Main-Phase model never had to begin with' (in the rationale text) while ELSEWHERE (rule_chronology.areas[0]) the SAME packet said the original rules DID have continuation after Battle inside the single Main Phase - a direct internal contradiction.
corrected_claims.correction: RESOLVED in favor of the correct reading, which the prior packet had half-right and half-wrong in two different places. The original Starter Box rulebook states explicitly: 'Even when the Battle Phase is over, as long as you do not move to the End Phase, it remains the Main Phase' - i.e. there was no phase called 'Main Phase 2', but play COULD continue in the single Main Phase after Battle Phase ended, before the player chose to end their turn. DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 REMOVES this legal post-battle action window entirely, which is the opposite of what the historical rule preserved - so DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 is HISTORICALLY WRONG for this ruleset, not an approximation of it. The correct engine representation is DEFAULT_OMISSION: leave DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 unset, and the modern MP1->BP->MP2->EP flow already reproduces the historical substance (continued action after Battle, before End Phase) even though the engine internally still labels that window 'Main Phase 2', a presentational difference no 1999-era card mechanic could ever have depended on.

corrected_claims.prior_claim: rule_chronology.areas included 'Hand size limit / discard at end of turn' and 'Tribute/Advance Summon requirements' both marked PROVEN 'from the original rulebook (first printing)'.
corrected_claims.correction: WRONG for the Starter Box tier. The original Starter Box rulebook contains NO hand-size limit or end-of-turn discard rule of any kind, and NO tribute/sacrifice cost for summoning any monster regardless of Level - every monster used the same free one-per-turn placement procedure. Both are correctly downgraded to UNKNOWN at the Starter Box tier (an absence-based finding, not an under-sourced guess). Separately, and NEWLY established in this corrective pass: there is meaningful secondary evidence that Tribute Summon (生け贄召喚, Level 5-6 = 1 Tribute, Level 7+ = 2 Tributes) and the other Expert Rules-era changes were in force generally before Tokyo Dome - but the exact 1999-05-05 transition date remains a STRONG_SECONDARY_RECONSTRUCTION, not PROVEN, for the later-1999 tier (matching the evidence_matrix's own later_1999_evidence_status for this row). The publication date of the 'Official Guide Starter Book' on 1999-05-05 is well supported (four independent sources), but the claim that this specific book is what introduced Expert Rules/Tribute Summon, and that 1999-05-05 is therefore the rule's exact effective date, remains unverified - no source in this research chain has actually inspected/quoted the book's own content confirming it. Do not read 'after_change as of 1999-08-26' (recorded in the evidence matrix's later_1999_effective_bounds field for this row) as a proven effective date - it is the best current hypothesis for the transition window, not a confirmed boundary. The hand-size limit was NOT introduced until the later 'New Expert Rules' (Series 2, from 2000 onward) - i.e. it almost certainly POSTDATES Tokyo Dome entirely, a materially different and stronger conclusion than 'merely unproven'.

change_boundary_before_tokyo_dome.core_question: Which rules had definitely changed by August 26, 1999? (NOT: what did 1999 rules generally look like?)
change_boundary_before_tokyo_dome.answer: Exactly one revision, the 'Expert Rules' revision, remains the best-supported candidate for a rules change between the original Starter Box (~March 1999) and Tokyo Dome (August 26, 1999). This pass located and personally inspected the actual 1999 Official Guide Starter Book scan: its pages 107-109 directly document the three Expert Rules changes (Tributes, hand-based Fusion materials, and any-number turn use of Magic cards). The guide's 1999-05-05 publication date anchors the existence of that documented rules tier by publication. The exact effective date for ordinary OCG play remains STRONG_SECONDARY_RECONSTRUCTION / SUPPORTED_BUT_INCOMPLETE: the guide says tournaments may adopt the rules, not that every OCG duel or Tokyo Dome adopted them on publication day. Whether Tokyo Dome specifically enforced them remains UNKNOWN.

This supersedes the earlier, weaker framing that rested mainly on an uncited 'Series 1 vs Series 2' blog claim.)

event_day_pool_reassessment.prior_verdict: No evidence any Aug-26-distributed card was legal in decks played that same day; Gate Guardian specifically could not have been Fusion Summoned using only pre-event-pool cards; certified pre-event 370-card, 1999-08-25 pool preserved unchanged.
event_day_pool_reassessment.new_finding: PERSONALLY VERIFIED by the adjudicator via two independent, directly-cross-referenced Yugipedia pages (Premium Pack (Japanese): jp_release_date = August 26, 1999, 'released in Japan on August 26, 1999 at the ... Duelist Legend in Tokyo Dome tournament'; Exodia the Forbidden One: earliest Japanese OCG printing listed as 'Premium Pack (Japanese)'). This is a materially different and more striking case than Gate Guardian: Exodia the Forbidden One - the FIFTH and final Forbidden One piece, without which the Exodia win_condition was categorically impossible in any OCG deck regardless of format or ruleset - was not available in Japan AT ALL before August 26, 1999. The translator's own footnote on the original Starter Box rulebook confirms these cards 'didn't even exist yet' as printed cards when that rulebook was written. Even the other four Forbidden One pieces were only completed as a printable set by 1999-08-05 (per the swarm's Agent B research), three weeks before Tokyo Dome - so the Exodia win condition, while textually PROVEN as a rule from the very first rulebook, was PRACTICALLY UNREACHABLE in real OCG play until the exact date this proposed format is named for, and even then only for a small number of attendees given the chaotic, halted distribution documented in event_disruption_reassessment.
event_day_pool_reassessment.does_this_change_the_pool_recommendation: NO. Exodia the Forbidden One remains correctly excluded from the certified pre-event 1999-08-25 370-card pool, consistent with the existing certification. This finding does not argue for extending the pool to include Aug-26 cards - if anything it reinforces the prior pass's caution about event-day legality, since even the one Aug-26 card most central to a 'complete' Tokyo Dome experience (the Exodia piece) was only reachable by a small, chaotic subset of attendees that day, not a reliable feature of 'the format as played'. It is reported here as important historical CONTEXT for any future canonical-format decision about event-day cards, not as a reason to alter the certified pool.

restriction_list_current._read_me_first: This is now the SOLE current representation of restriction-list research. It splits two concepts the prior pass conflated into one field: research_confidence (what we currently believe happened, and how strongly) and canonicalization_status (whether that belief is strong enough to safely encode a banlist). These can and do diverge - research_confidence has genuinely improved this session (personal inspection of the Master Guide page itself), but canonicalization_status remains BLOCKING regardless, because nobody in this research chain has inspected a contemporaneous 1999 document, only a 2004 retrospective. UPDATED 2026-08-30: further split into content_status, scope_status, and effective_date_status - three axes that must never be conflated (a source proving card content does not thereby prove scope; a publication date is not an effective date). See contemporaneous_source_investigation_2026_08_30 for the new evidence (a V Jump 1999-09 page image and an independently-archived fan chronology) that materially strengthened all three axes without fully resolving canonicalization_status, which remains UNRESOLVED_BLOCKING for reasons narrower and more specific than before. FURTHER RE-DERIVED 2026-08-30 (session 5): the three-axis model above was itself re-examined against what an actual August-26-Tokyo-Dome-snapshot banlist artifact requires (schemas/banlist.schema.json, retroformats/validate.py, retroformats/lflist.py - see banlist_artifact_requirements_2026_08_30_session5), rather than assumed correct. Finding: scope_status and effective_date_status each bundled one LOAD-BEARING proposition with one that is genuinely non-blocking for this specific artifact. Replaced with SIX axes: content_membership_status, content_completeness_status, target_event_applicability_status, and source_authentication_status are LOAD-BEARING (canonicalization_status derives from these four only); outer_scope_status (the old H2-vs-H3 question) and first_effective_date_status (the true historical origin date, as opposed to a defensible value <= the event snapshot) are EXPLICITLY NON-BLOCKING - demonstrated, not asserted, in banlist_artifact_requirements_2026_08_30_session5.critical_logical_test. Do not read a non-blocking axis staying UNRESOLVED_NONBLOCKING as a remaining canonicalization obstacle; it mechanically is not one. The central rule of this re-derivation: a historical uncertainty is a canonicalization blocker only if resolving it could change the artifact being represented. CORRECTED 2026-08-30 (session 6): the session-5 six-axis split above used an insufficient test for 'non-blocking' - whether generated lflist bytes would change - and wrongly excluded outer_scope_status and first_effective_date_status on that basis. A corrective re-derivation (banlist_artifact_requirements_2026_08_30_session6) found both are genuinely load-bearing after all: effective_date is documented by schemas/banlist.schema.json to mean the TRUE take-effect date, not a defensible stand-in value, and outer scope (H2 vs H3) determines whether representing this restriction as an ordinary region-scoped banlist object would itself misrepresent a one-event rule as a general regional policy. A NEW seventh axis, schema_representability_status, was added and found independently BLOCKING: the current banlist schema has no field for event/tournament scope at all. ALL SEVEN axes (content_membership_status, content_completeness_status, target_event_applicability_status, source_authentication_status, outer_scope_status, first_effective_date_status, schema_representability_status) are now load-bearing; none is excluded. The central rule is REFINED, not abandoned: a historical uncertainty is a canonicalization blocker only if resolving it could change a historical fact ASSERTED OR IMPLIED by the canonical artifact - which is a STRONGER, and different, test than 'would the generated bytes differ.' Mechanical representability (the validator accepts a value, the builder ignores a field) is not the same thing as semantic correctness (the recorded value is true, and the object's own shape honestly represents what kind of fact it is). CORRECTED AGAIN 2026-08-30 (session 7), two further errors: (1) session 6's own justification for schema_representability_status conflated H3 ('other tournament-specific scope') with H1 ('general OCG list') - outer_scope_status is now split into scope_class_status (S1: general-regional H1 vs tournament-specific H2-or-H3 - the proposition that actually determines schema representability) and tournament_extent_status (S2: given tournament-specific, H2-vs-H3 - a refinement of S1, not a substitute), with schema_representability_status re-modelled as DERIVED from scope_class_status via an explicit state machine (see canonicalization_status.derived_axes), not an eighth independent checkbox. (2) Separately, target_recommendation.snapshot had held 1999-08-25 (the pool-cutoff-motivated day BEFORE the event) rather than the format's own defining-event date (1999-08-26) that schemas/format.schema.json and this repo's own Edison precedent document snapshot to mean - corrected to 1999-08-26, with a new target_recommendation.pool_cutoff field preserving 1999-08-25 separately; mechanically re-verified this changes zero errata selections across the full 296-record corpus. See temporal_model_2026_08_30_session7 for the full T1-T8 temporal decomposition this correction is built on. canonicalization_status remains UNRESOLVED_BLOCKING throughout - both corrections clarify structure, neither removes a blocking reason.

The SIX genuinely independent, evidence-based, load-bearing propositions are content_membership_status, content_completeness_status, target_event_applicability_status, source_authentication_status, scope_class_status, and first_effective_date_status - this is now a literal, uncaveated match between load_bearing_axes and 'six genuinely independent propositions', not an approximation carrying an unexplained seventh member. schema_representability_status ITSELF remains modelled as DERIVED/CONDITIONAL on scope_class_status (see cs.derived_axes above), not as an independent checkbox - it is currently BLOCKING because scope_class_status is UNRESOLVED with an evidentiary lean AGAINST H1, the only branch of its state machine that would resolve it. canonicalization_status therefore remains UNRESOLVED_BLOCKING - both corrections change WHICH exact propositions are independently load-bearing and clarify two dependencies; neither removes any blocking reason. master_guide_p84_verification.method: Yugipedia's citation for this restriction list links a specific uploaded image file, Media:Master Guide p84.jpg, discovered by the adjudicator via the MediaWiki API (action=query&prop=revisions with rvslots=main&rvprop=content on the 'August 1999 Lists' page). The adjudicator resolved the direct image URL via the API's imageinfo endpoint (action=query&titles=File:Master Guide p84.jpg&prop=imageinfo&iiprop=url|timestamp|user|comment|size), downloaded the file directly, confirmed the downloaded file's byte size and pixel dimensions matched the API's own metadata exactly (a basic integrity check that the file was not corrupted or substituted in transit), and then personally viewed the image directly (not via any AI image-description intermediary - the adjudicator itself is a multimodal model and read the page visually).
master_guide_p84_verification.what_is_actually_visible: The page is headed '>>> 1999年2月〜8月' ('1999, February through August') under the chapter title 'DECK BEST SELECTION' ('デッキベストセレクション', matching Yugipedia's cited chapter name exactly), with the page footer 'MASTER GUIDE | Yu-Gi-Oh! OCG | 084'. A boxed legend near the top-left is headed '【1999年8月26日大会限定　制限・禁止カード一覧】' ('[August 26, 1999 tournament-limited restriction/forbidden card list]'). Below it: 禁止カード (Forbidden card) = なし (none); 制限カード (Restricted/Limited card) = サンダー・ボルト (Thunder Bolt/Raigeki), ブラック・ホール (Black Hole/Dark Hole), 落とし穴 (Trap Hole); 準制限カード (Semi-Limited card) = なし (none). A subheading reads '初の制限カードはこの3枚!' ('The first-ever restricted cards are these 3!'). Body text explains 'サンダー・ボルト' and 'ブラック・ホール' were powerful even at the time, and that 'Trap Hole' was restricted likely to encourage monster-vs-monster combat - then states '落とし穴は、すぐに制限が解除されている' ('Trap Hole had its restriction lifted again soon after'), a genuinely new finding not previously known to this research chain. Two boxed card images are labeled '★ Restriction card >>>' (Black Hole and Thunder Bolt/Raigeki). A separate box discusses period-notable cards (Trap Hole, Blue-Eyes White Dragon) including an incidental mention that Blue-Eyes 'was normally Summoned with 2 Tributes' at the time this retrospective page describes - consistent with, though not independent proof of, Tribute Summon being an established practice by the Feb-Aug 1999 window this specific page covers. The rest of the page lists five 'trending deck' archetypes from the period, not directly relevant to rules research.
master_guide_p84_verification.quotation_vs_interpretation: All Japanese text quoted above is transcribed directly from what is visually legible in the scan, by the adjudicator's own reading - not relayed through Yugipedia's citation or any other secondary description. English glosses immediately following each quoted phrase are the adjudicator's own translation, clearly distinguished from the quoted original. The identification of this as 'a genuinely new finding' (the Trap Hole lift) and the assessment of what this does/does not establish are the adjudicator's own interpretation, kept separate from the direct transcription above.
master_guide_p84_verification.what_this_does_not_establish: This is Shueisha's own 2004 retrospective account, written five years after the event, not a 1999 primary document - it does not by itself prove this is how Konami itself officially framed the restriction in 1999, only how a major official-adjacent publisher's 2004 historical retrospective characterizes it. It does not establish whether the restriction was ever also applied more broadly (e.g. at qualifying rounds before the Tokyo Dome finals specifically) - the page's own header language ('tournament-limited') argues against a broader reading, but does not conclusively rule out every alternative framing. Per this reasoning, canonicalization_status above remains BLOCKING despite this genuine confidence upgrade.

scope_hypotheses._source: Merged from primary_source_resolution_2026_08_29 during 2026-08-29 consolidation - this is now the sole location for this reasoning.

hypotheses.label: general OCG list
hypotheses.assessment: The list content is repeated as an early OCG restriction list, but the inspected later sources do not supply a contemporaneous Konami document proving nationwide ordinary-play scope.

hypotheses.label: Tokyo Dome/event-only list
hypotheses.assessment: The 2004 Shueisha Master Guide scan reproduced by Yugipedia has the header '1999年8月26日大会限定 制限・禁止カード一覧', but that is a later retrospective, not a contemporaneous event document. The specialist article relays an additional third-party claim and is hedged. UPDATED 2026-08-30: now also supported by a page image attributed to V Jump 1999-09 and an independently-archived-since-2002 fan chronology, both personally inspected this session - both use tournament-scoped language, strengthening the case against H1 (general OCG list), but neither pins the boundary to the August 26 FINALS specifically as opposed to the whole national tournament run (see H3) - status remains UNRESOLVED for the precise H2-vs-H3 boundary, though the broader tournament-vs-general question is now well-supported.

hypotheses.label: other tournament-specific scope
hypotheses.assessment: Tournament-oriented cataloguing exists, but no inspected primary or period regulation identifies the exact population of tournaments to which the three-card list applied. UPDATED 2026-08-30: the V Jump 1999-09 page image (personally inspected) discusses the restriction inside a passage explicitly about deck preparation DURING ONGOING QUALIFIERS ('予選のまっただ中'), framing it as discussion occurring during qualifiers. REVISED 2026-08-30 after adversarial review and personal re-examination of the page image: this proves the restriction was being publicly DISCUSSED while qualifiers were running, not that it APPLIED to qualifying matches - a reader could be reading advance notice of an eventual finals-only rule during qualifiers just as easily as reading about a rule already live. This passage is therefore NOT treated as a lean toward H3 over H2 - see target_event_applicability_status and tournament_extent_status (S2, 2026-08-30 session-7 rename of outer_scope_status) for the full walk-back. Status remains genuinely UNRESOLVED between H2 and H3, not H3-favored.

hypotheses.label: retrospective reconstruction
hypotheses.assessment: The surviving online evidence is downstream and internally divergent. This remains a live explanation, not a proven historical scope. UPDATED 2026-08-30: the home.att.ne.jp fan chronology and the V Jump page image are both now-inspected, non-circular sources that converge with Master Guide on content and broad scope direction - this materially weakens (without eliminating) H4 as the LEADING explanation, since three sources with a distinct underlying origin agreeing - two independently-authored retrospectives (Master Guide, home.att.ne.jp) plus one candidate primary object (the V Jump issue itself) - is harder to explain as pure downstream reconstruction than the single-source situation this hypothesis was originally framed against. REVISED 2026-08-30 (session 5) after adversarial review: this is deliberately NOT phrased as 'three independently-authored sources' - the V Jump object's own modern rediscovery (ygoldschool.com, 2021) is not demonstrated independent of the earlier comment (マルコヴィッチ, 2020) that first named the same issue, so only 2 of the 3 groups are demonstrated independent in authorship; see content_membership_status (2026-08-30 session-5 rename) and provenance_independence_assessment.cross_group_convergence.

scope_hypotheses.provenance_finding: The phrase equivalent to '1999-08-26 tournament-limited' was traced in this pass to the later Master Guide page 84 wording as surfaced by the current Yugipedia citation. The original 1999 list sheet or event regulation behind that retrospective was not located. Repeated modern headers therefore do not count as independent contemporaneous corroboration. UPDATED 2026-08-30: two additional sources were found and personally inspected that are NOT downstream of the Master Guide retrospective - a page image attributed to V Jump 1999-09 (ygoldschool.com) and a fan chronology independently archived since 2002-10 (home.att.ne.jp) - see contemporaneous_source_investigation_2026_08_30. Repeated modern headers STILL do not count as independent corroboration on their own; what changed is that these two additions are not repetitions of the Master Guide header - they rest on a distinct underlying origin (one independently-authored retrospective, home.att.ne.jp; one candidate PRIMARY historical object, V Jump 1999-09) rather than being repostings of Master Guide's own claim. REVISED 2026-08-30 (session 5): 'separately-authored' overclaimed the V Jump find specifically - its own modern hosting (ygoldschool.com) is not demonstrated independent of the earlier comment that first named the same issue; see content_membership_status (2026-08-30 session-5 rename) and provenance_independence_assessment for the precise, per-group independence bookkeeping.
scope_hypotheses.what_would_close_it: A contemporaneous 1999 Konami rule/list sheet, tournament programme, entry regulation, or period magazine/newspaper reproduction that states both the three card entries and their scope/effective event.

This section records what was actually found, personally inspected, and adjudicated - the V Jump lead, an independent fan restriction-list chronology, and a related Valuable Book 1 finding, each kept to exactly the proposition its own evidence supports.

image_personally_inspected.article_heading: 要注意!! (yōchūi!! - 'Important warning!!'), inside a larger feature headed with the event's official Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters '決闘者伝説 The Legend of Duelist in TOKYO DOME' logo/branding.
exact_japanese_text_transcribed: 使用枚数が制限されたカードたち！ (Cards whose usage count has been RESTRICTED!)

左に並んでいる3種類のカードたち…。なんとこれらは、『決闘者伝説』では1枚ずつしかデッキに入れることができないのだ!! じゅうぶん気をつけよう! (The 3 types of cards lined up on the left... Amazingly, these can only be included ONE COPY EACH in a deck AT 'Duelist Legend'!! Be very careful!)
card labels: 「落とし穴」(Trap Hole), 「ブラック・ホール」(Black Hole/Dark Hole), 「サンダー・ボルト」(Thunder Bolt/Raigeki)
elsewhere on the same page: 決闘は作戦が大事なんだ！(Dueling is all about strategy!) - character dialogue, flavour text

採用ルールは「エキスパートルール」(The adopted rule is 'Expert Rules') - 4大特徴 (4 major features): tribute summon for high-level monsters, Magic cards can be set face-down, Magic & Trap cards usable consecutively, Fusion directly from hand
試合条件 (Match conditions): deck 40+ cards, side deck 10 cards, 8000 LP, 20-min duels, best-of-3 match, 10-min interval between duels for side-deck adjustment

ただいま『決闘者伝説』の全国大会出場権をかけた予選のまっただ中っ!! 大会は使用Cの枚数制限などがあるので、試合用のデッキを作っておこう! (Right now, [we are] in the middle of qualifiers for a spot in the 'Duelist Legend' national tournament!! Since the TOURNAMENT has restrictions on the number of cards (C) usable, let's prepare a match-ready deck!)

vjump_1999_09_investigation.translated_summary: A period-magazine-style game-guide page (character art, colour-coded boxes, furigana reading guides, consistent with 1999 Shonen Jump/V Jump house style) explains Expert Rules and match conditions for the upcoming Tokyo Dome tournament, and separately warns that Trap Hole, Black Hole, and Thunder Bolt are each restricted to 1 copy per deck 'at Duelist Legend' - explicitly tying the restriction to the event by name, inside a passage written while qualifiers were still ongoing (i.e. before the August 26 finals).
vjump_1999_09_investigation.text_type: Editorial narration / player-facing game-guide copy (character-dialogue style, typical of V Jump's strategy-article format) - NOT a verbatim Konami press release or tournament regulation document quoted in full; NOT a direct Konami quotation as far as is visible in the recovered crop.
vjump_1999_09_investigation.contradicts_master_guide: Does not flatly contradict Master Guide's card content or general tournament-scoped framing, but is in SLIGHT TENSION on the precise scope boundary (see tournament_extent_status.what_remains_unresolved (S2, 2026-08-30 session-7 rename of outer_scope_status)) - this tension is preserved, not force-reconciled, per this session's explicit instruction.
vjump_1999_09_investigation.authenticity_caveats: This image is hosted by exactly ONE source found in this research chain (ygoldschool.com); no independent second hosting of the same image, and no independent confirmation of its issue/date beyond the hosting blog's own caption, were located. Unlike the Official Guide Starter Book scan elsewhere in this packet (personally cross-checked against archive.org's own file-size/hash metadata), this image's chain of custody from the physical 1999 magazine to this specific JPEG is NOT independently documented. Treated accordingly as SUPPORTED_BUT_INCOMPLETE evidence, not PROVEN, despite being personally inspected.

home_att_puppiy_chronology_investigation.exact_japanese_text_of_1999_entry: ◆1999年7月〜8月　１回目の大会（東京ドーム）用に発表された制限　●制限カード　１枚制限　以下のカードはデッキに１枚まで。（サイドデッキ含む）「サンダー・ボルト」「ブラック・ホール」「落とし穴」
home_att_puppiy_chronology_investigation.translated: '1999, July-August: the restriction announced for the 1st tournament (Tokyo Dome). Restricted cards, 1-copy limit: the following cards are limited to 1 in the deck (including the side deck): Thunder Bolt, Black Hole, Trap Hole.'
home_att_puppiy_chronology_investigation.structural_context: This is the OLDEST (chronologically first) entry in an extensive, otherwise well-corroborated chronology of every OCG restriction-list revision from 1999 through 2002-05-01 that the page author personally tracked and dated (each subsequent revision explains what changed and often why, e.g. tied to specific product releases). The page explicitly labels the 1999 entry as being for the '１回目の大会' (1st tournament) and the 2000 February-March entry as the '２回目の大会' (2nd tournament) restriction, before a general list was formally published in Weekly Jump at the start of what the page calls 'Series 2' (2000-04-01) - i.e. this source independently describes the SAME pattern already suspected elsewhere in this research chain: an initial tournament-specific restriction, later formalized into a general list. The page states plainly, as of its most recent (2002-05-01) entry, that no card had EVER been forbidden in OCG history up to that point (禁止カードは今のところ１枚も出ていない) - independently checkable against real Yu-Gi-Oh! OCG history and consistent with it, lending the page's overall care/accuracy real weight.
home_att_puppiy_chronology_investigation.citation_for_its_own_1999_entry: None given. Unlike several later entries (which tie a revision to 'X product released 1 month prior'), the 1999年7月〜8月 entry cites no specific magazine, product, or date-anchor of its own. It is NOT itself confirmable as a magazine scan or primary document - it is a specialist's personal chronology, whose own sourcing for this earliest entry is unstated.
home_att_puppiy_chronology_investigation.yugipedia_citation_title_mismatch_resolv: Investigated per this session's explicit instruction to revisit Yugipedia's old citation, which described this page's title as 'Forbidden/Limited Card Lists May 15, 2000.' Personally checked the page's actual <title> HTML tag at both inspected snapshots (2002-10, 2005-12): both read '遊戯王ＯＣＧ【資料庫】３/その他' (Yu-Gi-Oh OCG [Archive] 3/Other) - NOT 'Forbidden/Limited Card Lists May 15, 2000.' The '2000年5月15日' string does appear WITHIN the page as one of many dated chronology-section headings (◆2000年5月15日), not as the page's own title. The most likely explanation is that the citing Yugipedia editor (2017) used a descriptive gloss of their own rather than the page's literal title - not evidence that the page itself is mistitled or that its content is unreliable.

valuable_book_1_corroboration.product_status: Already a certified product in this repository's own OCG release ledger ('Valuable Book 1 promos', dated 1999-08-20, source_id konami-card-history) - within the 370-card candidate pool's cutoff window, 6 days before Tokyo Dome.
valuable_book_1_corroboration.reported_finding: A named commenter (めう, on yugioh-history.com, 2021-07-06) reports personally checking their own physical copy of The Valuable Book 1: the book's Expert Rules explanation pages contain NO explicit restriction-card list or notation, but EVERY sample deck recipe printed in the book caps Thunder Bolt, Black Hole, and Trap Hole at exactly 1 copy each - including in decks that would otherwise clearly benefit from more copies (a Trap-heavy deck running 3x of an unrelated card still uses only 1 Trap Hole; a burn-focused deck running 3x Pot of Greed still uses only 1 Thunder Bolt). The commenter's own inference: Konami's publishing pipeline was already privately observing a 1-copy cap for these 3 cards by 1999-08-20, before any explicit public restriction notice appeared in print, consistent with a restriction being announced/formalized very close to (at or shortly before) the August 26 event.
valuable_book_1_corroboration.verification_status: NOT personally verified by the final adjudicator - no accessible scan of Valuable Book 1's interior pages was located this session (ocg-card.com's card-list page for this product returned only placeholder images, not actual scans, when fetched). Recorded as a specific, checkable, named-individual's account of an already-certified physical product, not as directly-inspected primary evidence. A future session with access to the physical book or a genuine scan could either confirm or refute this account directly.

lane1_surugaya_date_discrepancy.finding: The Suruga-ya catalogue listing for the exact issue was located: item ZNON5070, ゲーム雑誌付録付)Vジャンプ 1999年9月号 ゲーム (V Jump, September 1999 issue, with appendix), publisher Shueisha, 'Released date' field = 01 Sep 1999.
lane1_surugaya_date_discrepancy.test_performed: Six V Jump back-issue listings across two years and five different calendar months (Feb 1998 ZNON5058, Mar 1998 ZNON5059, May 1999 ZNON4176, Aug 1999 ZNON5069, Sep 1999 ZNON5070, Nov 1999 ZNON5071) were compared. lane1_surugaya_date_discrepancy.conclusion: This is conclusive: a genuine, individually-researched street date could not plausibly land on the 1st for six unrelated issues across five different months and two years. Suruga-ya's 'Released date' field for old magazine back-issues is a DATA-ENTRY CONVENTION defaulting to YYYY-MM-01 (year+month tracked, day padded), not a researched per-issue street date. This neither confirms nor contradicts the ~1999-07-21 on-sale inference (V Jump's general monthly-21st convention) - it is simply not evidentiary on that question either way, and must not be read as conflicting with it.

phase_a_effective_date_semantics.A1_validator_mechanics: retroformats/validate.py's _validate_format (~line 1715-1721): `eff = self._date(banlist.effective_date)`; `if eff and snapshot and not (eff <= snapshot): error(...)`; symmetrically `superseded < snapshot fails`. This is a NECESSARY-but-not-sufficient consistency check: it verifies the format's chosen snapshot date falls inside the banlist's OWN DECLARED window. It does NOT and CANNOT verify the declared window is historically accurate - it has no access to ground truth, only to what this repository itself wrote into effective_date. A wrong-but-internally-consistent date passes this check exactly as well as a correct one.
phase_a_effective_date_semantics.A2_documented_semantic_meaning: schemas/banlist.schema.json's OWN description (not the validator, the schema's stated meaning): 'One historical Forbidden/Limited list AS IT TOOK EFFECT ON A GIVEN DATE.' effective_date's own $ref is a bare isoDate with no hedging language anywhere ('known by', 'attested by', 'at least by') - it is presented as THE date, full stop. superseded_by_date is described the same way: 'Date the next list TOOK EFFECT, if known' - again 'took effect,' not 'is known to have changed by.' docs/format-schema.md states the mechanical PURPOSE this serves: 'effective_date and superseded_by_date let the validator prove the list was ACTUALLY in force on a format's snapshot date' - the word 'actually' is doing real work here: the validator's proof is only meaningful as a TRUE historical claim if the underlying date IS the true one; a deliberately-substituted-but-safe date would make the validator's 'proof' formally valid but historically hollow, defeating the documented purpose rather than fulfilling it. Also load-bearing: both the schema description AND docs/format-schema.md independently describe banlists as 'region-scoped facts, independent of formats' / 'format-independent data: several formats may reference the same snapshot' - i.e. effective_date is meant to be a standalone historical fact about the real-world policy document/decision, not a value tuned to whichever format happens to reference it. CONCLUSION: the documented semantic meaning is the TRUE, ACTUAL date this list came into force - not a conservative lower-bound attestation. Nothing in the schema or docs supports a 'known to be in force by' reading.
phase_a_effective_date_semantics.A3_builder_consumption: retroformats/lflist.py: confirmed again this session (grep for 'effective_date' returns zero hits in this file). build_lflist()/_build_whitelist() read only banlist.entries and the format's own errata policy. effective_date is read ONLY by validate.py, for the A1 consistency check.
phase_a_effective_date_semantics.A4_does_nonconsumption_weaken_A2: NO - explicitly re-examined rather than assumed, per this pass's instruction. A field's semantic meaning is fixed by its schema description and project documentation (a design-level contract), not by which downstream process happens to read it (a runtime-level fact). Other fields in this same schema - notes, sources, completeness - are also not consumed by the builder, and nobody would argue THEY are therefore meaningless or reinterpretable; the same reasoning applies to effective_date. If anything, the opposite argument holds slightly more weight: this project specifically built validator machinery to check this field's internal consistency, which is a stronger signal the field is treated as semantically load-bearing by the project's own design, not evidence it is a free variable. SESSION 5'S ERROR, NAMED PRECISELY: it treated 'the validator cannot detect a wrong-but-earlier true date' as license to write a value chosen for mechanical safety (the snapshot date) rather than historical accuracy (the researched true date) - conflating 'undetectable by current tooling' with 'semantically permitted.' Those are not the same claim, and only the schema's own documented meaning (A2) settles which is intended.

banlist_artifact_requirements_2026_08_30.confronting_the_hypothetical: Historical truth: list began applying 1999-07-21. Target format snapshot: 1999-08-26. Canonical banlist writes effective_date = 1999-08-26. Per A2, this record WOULD truthfully mean only one thing: 'this list took effect on 1999-08-26' - and if the true date is 1999-07-21, that recorded claim is FALSE, not conservative. The repository's current contract does NOT permit a 'known to be in force by this date' reading of effective_date - that is a genuinely different proposition, and using the existing field to carry it would silently redefine a mature canonical field's meaning in research prose, which this pass was explicitly told not to do.
banlist_artifact_requirements_2026_08_30.goat_precedent_reexamined: formats/2005-04-goat/format.json + data/banlists/tcg/2005-04.json: effective_date = '2005-04-01', with the banlist's own notes admitting 'the effective/superseded dates are the community-documented April 1 / October 1 2005 TCG list boundaries and also need a primary citation' plus a TODO to 'cross-check against the April 2005 TCG list as published (Yugipedia) and upgrade completeness.' PRECISE CLAIM THIS PROVES: the project accepts populating effective_date at a LOWER EVIDENTIARY TIER (community consensus, not a personally-verified primary Konami/UDE document) as long as the recorded value is still the researchers' genuine belief about the TRUE effective date, with an explicit intent to upgrade the EVIDENCE for that same claimed date later. This is a confidence-tier compromise on ONE proposition (what date is true), not license to substitute a DIFFERENT, more convenient date. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: that deliberately writing a later, mechanically-safer date INSTEAD OF the researched true date is acceptable - GOAT's April 1 value is not understood by anyone in this project to be a deliberate stand-in for some other, earlier or later, actually-true date; it is the believed-true date itself, just imperfectly sourced. Session 5's proposed 'use 1999-08-26 instead of the ~1999-07-21 lead we actually have' move has no analogue in the GOAT precedent - it is a categorically different kind of substitution.
banlist_artifact_requirements_2026_08_30.phase_b_new_date_concept_adjudication: If this project needs to represent 'we know this restriction was definitely in force on/by 1999-08-26, but we do not know when it first took effect' - is effective_date the right field for that? NO, per Phase A: effective_date is documented to mean the true take-effect date, not a lower attestation bound. A genuinely different concept (e.g. an attested_in_force_by field, or an evidence-bound/uncertainty structure distinct from effective_date) WOULD be needed to encode that weaker claim truthfully. THIS PASS DOES NOT ADD OR RENAME ANY SCHEMA FIELD - per explicit instruction, a schema change requires a separate, deliberately-reviewed design task, and this corrective pass's job is to correctly identify the gap, not casually patch it. RECORDED AS A REPRESENTABILITY BLOCKER: the current schema cannot truthfully encode 'known in force by X, true start unknown' - see schema_representability_status.

phase_c_outer_scope_reexamined.the_insufficient_prior_test: Session 5 asked only 'would H2 vs H3 change banlist.entries or force a different effective_date value?' and, finding no, concluded outer scope was non-blocking. phase_c_outer_scope_reexamined.what_a_canonical_banlist_object_structur: schemas/banlist.schema.json: id pattern '^(tcg|ocg|ww)-[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}$', matching file path data/banlists/<region>/<yyyy>-<mm>.json - i.e. REGION + YEAR-MONTH, with no event/tournament-level field anywhere in the schema. region is a 3-value enum (TCG/OCG/Worldwide) from common.schema.json - no finer scope granularity exists. The schema's own description AND docs/format-schema.md both independently describe banlists as 'region-scoped facts... several formats may reference the same snapshot' - REUSABILITY across formats is presented as a designed-in FEATURE, not an incidental possibility. Every banlist actually in this repository (GOAT tcg-2005-04, Edison tcg-2010-03, Tengu tcg-2011-09) is a genuine, broadly-applicable REGIONAL policy document - the kind of list virtually every tournament/player in that region during that window was expected to use. There is NO existing precedent in this repository for a narrowly-scoped, single-event-only banlist.
phase_c_outer_scope_reexamined.does_h2_vs_h3_change_an_asserted_or_impl: YES. If H2 is true (Tokyo Dome finals only, never a general OCG policy), encoding this restriction as an ordinary data/banlists/ocg/1999-08.json with region: 'OCG' would - by the schema's OWN stated semantics ('region-scoped fact... several formats may reference the same snapshot') - assert that this 3-card limit was THE OCG region's general Forbidden/Limited policy during August 1999, indistinguishable in FORM from GOAT/Edison/Tengu's genuine broad regional lists. That would be a substantive misrepresentation if ordinary OCG play at the time had no such restriction outside this one tournament. A future, unrelated August-1999 OCG format could legitimately (and wrongly) reuse this banlist as the general regional list, exactly because nothing in the object's own identity signals narrower scope - this is the concrete 'could another future format incorrectly reuse the artifact' risk this pass asked about, and it is real, not hypothetical. If H3 is true (a genuinely broader, if early/short-lived, regional policy - closer in kind to how GOAT/Edison/Tengu are already modeled), representing it as an ordinary region-scoped banlist would be comparatively defensible. The choice between H2 and H3 therefore determines whether the CURRENT schema shape is even an honest container for this fact, independent of what bytes get generated - exactly the distinction this pass's central principle draws.
phase_c_outer_scope_reexamined.where_could_event_scope_be_encoded_today: Checked format.schema.json: defining_events[] carries {name, date, sources} - free-text event descriptions on the FORMAT, not a scope qualifier on the BANLIST. chronology.previous/next are bare format-id strings. A format's own notes field COULD carry prose like 'this format's banlist is Tokyo-Dome-event-specific, not a general OCG list' - but per the banlist schema's own explicit 'several formats may reference the same snapshot' design, that caveat would live on ONE format's notes, not structurally travel with the banlist object itself; a second format referencing the same banlist id would inherit no such warning unless it separately repeated the same prose by hand. This is a fragile, unenforced mitigation, not a structural fix - checked and found insufficient, not assumed insufficient. GAP FOUND BY ADVERSARIAL REVIEW, ACCEPTED: this audit initially discussed only format.notes and missed that banlist.schema.json ALSO carries its own top-level 'notes' field (distinct from the per-entry entries[].notes), which - unlike format.notes - WOULD structurally travel with the banlist object on reuse, since it lives in the same JSON file every referencing format resolves to. Checked directly: this does not change the Outcome B conclusion, because banlist.notes is optional free text that retroformats/validate.py never reads or enforces - nothing stops a reusing format's author from simply not reading it, and the schema's own additionalProperties: false (line 8) means there is no way to add a MACHINE-CHECKABLE scope flag without an actual schema change. A human-readable caveat is a real, available partial mitigation (worth adding to any future canonicalized banlist regardless), but it is not the structural, validator-enforced fix this axis is tracking the absence of.
phase_c_outer_scope_reexamined.outcome: OUTCOME B (of the three the task pre-specified): the current banlist schema cannot faithfully distinguish a one-event restriction from a broader OCG regional restriction - there is no field for it, the id/region shape structurally implies general regional applicability, and no other canonical structure (defining_events, notes) closes the gap in an enforced way. This is recorded as a genuine schema_representability_status blocker (a NEW, explicit, seventh proposition - not folded into outer_scope_status, per this pass's instruction not to hide representability inside another axis) - NOT as a reason to design a new schema in this pass. H2-vs-H3 itself (outer_scope_status) is ALSO restored to load-bearing: even setting the schema-representability question aside, resolving H2-vs-H3 changes what historical claim the eventual artifact would need to assert, which is a fact about the artifact's truth, not merely about which bytes get generated.

banlist_artifact_requirements_2026_08_30.central_principle_applied: A fact can be irrelevant to generated bytes and still be essential to the historical truth of a canonical artifact. Both first_effective_date_status (Phase A/B) and outer_scope_status (Phase C) are exactly such facts: resolving either would not change dist/lflists' bytes, but each bears directly on whether a canonical banlist object, once created, would assert something true. Mechanical representability (the validator accepts it, the builder ignores it) is not the same thing as semantic correctness (the recorded value is true, and the object's very shape honestly represents what kind of fact it is).
